analysis.one_liner: Cuts the federal income tax rate on domestic manufacturing income to roughly 20 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Ron Kind with 8 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code to give companies that manufacture goods in the United States a large deduction equal to 50.5% of their domestic manufacturing income (43% for regular corporations), which would cut their effective income tax rate to about 20%. The deduction is capped at 25% of the company's "qualifying domestic investment," a base that includes the W-2 wages it pays workers plus certain equipment, energy, and research deductions. The bill contained no offsetting revenue increases, so the tax cut would be paid for by lower federal revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies with domestic manufacturing income — from large C corporations to partnerships and S corporations — would pay roughly 20% instead of the 27–31% effective rates cited in the bill's findings. The wage-and-investment cap means the biggest deductions flow to manufacturers with large domestic payrolls and equipment spending.

how_it_helps.text: Allows a deduction equal to 50.5% of domestic manufacturing income (43% for C corporations), effectively reducing the tax rate on that income to about 20%.

Caps the deduction at 25% of qualifying domestic investment — the sum of W-2 wages plus depreciation, energy-efficiency, and research deductions — tying the size of the break to domestic hiring and investment.

Excludes receipts from food and beverages prepared at retail establishments, and explicitly excludes oil, gas, mining property, electricity, and potable water from qualified property, targeting the break at goods production.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers as a whole, since the bill creates a large new deduction with no offsetting revenue provisions; non-manufacturing businesses also continue paying higher rates than manufacturers, making the code less even-handed.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no pay-fors: the new deduction would reduce federal revenue with nothing in the bill to replace it, adding to deficits or forcing later cuts or tax increases elsewhere.

The break is limited to companies with domestic manufacturing income, leaving service firms, retailers, and other employers at higher effective rates and inviting lobbying to expand who counts as a 'manufacturer.'
The wage-and-investment cap makes the deduction complex to administer and ties its value to accounting categories as much as to actual job creation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a substantial tax cut to one sector at a real cost to everyone else through lost federal revenue, with no offset. Its one defensible design feature — capping the deduction at a share of wages and domestic investment — pushes some of the benefit toward companies that actually employ people in the U.S., but it does not change the basic fact that this is a sector-specific rate cut without funding.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Kind (D-WI) introduced the Rebuilding American Manufacturing Act of 2015 on July 8, 2015, joined by 8 Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — is recorded before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers kept the revenue that a 20% manufacturing rate would have given away; domestic manufacturers, the intended beneficiaries, gained nothing because the bill never moved.

for.name: Rep. Ron Kind
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 8, 2015 and recruited 8 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 8 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Neal, Rangel, Pascrell, Larson, McDermott, Davis, and Levin.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republicans signed on; no votes were ever taken, so opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would cut their effective tax rate to about 20% with no offsetting revenue, so the cost of the break falls on federal taxpayers generally. The wage-linked cap would steer some benefit toward companies with large U.S. payrolls.
The bill explicitly excludes oil, gas, primary products, and mining property from qualified property, so these extractive industries would get no benefit from the manufacturing rate cut.
Software is qualified property, but video games rated M, AO, or RP are carved out of the deduction.
